He researched the industry and found the best seller among peers was Centrum, and retailers told him: Centrum didn't give the channel much margin, but it advertised heavily on TV all year and had great athlete endorsements, so consumers walked into the pharmacy and asked for it by name. Sali wanted to replicate that at Swisse. He started with Australia's national sport, cricket — the men's team captain, buying very short ad slots only during the hottest summer cricket broadcasts, so a limited budget could still appear at key moments. But the female-dominated sales channel wasn't impressed; one buyer didn't watch cricket and didn't know the player. He asked his mother what she liked to watch, she said a dance variety show, and the strategy pivoted to spoken endorsements inside entertainment content.

26:09 Selling health as a lifestyle
Swisse's bigger promotional push leaned on Oprah and Ellen, and signed actress Nicole Kidman for three years, extending its reach from Australia to the United States. By 2012 Swisse had 25 brand ambassadors, had shot more than 80 TV commercials in the previous 12 months, and reached annual revenue of A$183 million, with marketing spend of A$40-50 million a year — reportedly at one point the highest marketing spend of any consumer brand in Australia. Its ads didn't stress efficacy or ingredients; they mainly presented a state of being energetic, self-disciplined and good-looking — converting health into a lifestyle consumers aspire to. In 2012 Swisse took more than 20% market share in Australian supermarkets and more than 10% in pharmacies.

32:14 The growth was found in Chinese pharmacies
Swisse spent heavily on the US market without much success, and on returning home found that Swisse sold extremely well in pharmacies in Chinese-populated areas — some stores selling at ten times the level of an ordinary store — because students and Chinese migrants bought it in bulk to carry back to China or resell online, that is, daigou. Two policy shifts came in 2015: in March the Hangzhou cross-border e-commerce comprehensive pilot zone was approved, and in June China and Australia signed a free trade agreement, which took effect that December. The FTA mainly affects ordinary trade; Australian official statistics put the tariff on vitamins and supplements generally at 3% to 10%, while Black Moth itself estimated an average of 20%, and after the agreement it was said the rate could fall to zero within four years. Cross-border e-commerce runs through bonded warehouses, platforms buy in bulk, logistics time and cost drop sharply, and such goods are treated under the policy as for personal use, so they don't have to go through the supplement import registration and filing process.

35:16 The brand was bought; the impression stayed put
In September 2015 the Hong Kong-listed company Biostime completed the acquisition of a controlling stake in Swisse, and two years later completed a full buyout, a deal of about A$1.7 billion, or RMB 8.7 billion. For Swisse the deal carried little premium; for Biostime it added a large chunk of business revenue and imagination. All those Swisse ads in Hunan TV variety shows now are, in theory, a Chinese supplement company spending money, yet the brand can still say it is an Australian supplement brand, and consumers can still apply their old vague good impression of Australia to it — a large share of the acquisition's core value sits in brand goodwill.

item.title: Lenin Built the Terror Machine; Stalin Just Took It Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-empirehist-列宁设计了恐怖机器-斯大林只是接手了它/
item.description: The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.
item.content:encoded:
The secret police, the labour camps and the one-party system were all architecture Lenin left behind. What Stalin did was turn it into a personal instrument of power — the first thing he did as General Secretary was stuff his own people into key posts.

This episode gets the attribution of the Soviet terror system straight: it wasn't invented out of thin air by Stalin, it was a stage Lenin built and Stalin performed on. The back half, on Lenin's testament and the funeral details, is dense with information.

2:06 In 1917 Stalin was a man nobody noticed
The episode opens by recalling the impression left by the previous instalment: Stalin was a terrible speaker and a slow theorist, and nobody would have guessed he was the next dictator. Guest Giles Milton confirms that judgement and adds a key detail — Stalin rarely appeared in public and was not well known in Russia; he hated public speaking because his Georgian accent was so heavy. This explains how he was later able to accumulate power quietly: nobody treated him as a threat.

4:11 Churchill once wanted to wipe out the Red Army with gas
During the civil war, Britain, France, America and Japan all backed the Whites. Churchill, as Minister of Munitions in 1919, pushed Britain to send troops and weapons to Russia to fight the Reds. More striking still, Britain had developed a lethal chemical weapon late in the First World War, and Churchill thought it more humane than the bloody slaughter in the trenches, so he sent it to use against Trotsky's Red Army. Because of the atmospheric conditions in northern Russia the gas worked poorly, and the whole stock was eventually dumped into the White Sea. This history explains how hard it was when Churchill allied with Stalin in 1941 — he himself was one of the men who had wanted to get rid of Stalin back then.

9:27 The terror machine's architecture was Lenin's legacy
Many people put the Cheka, the labour camps and the one-party system down to Stalin, saying he built them while serving as a political commissar in the civil war. Giles argues this completely misunderstands Lenin's role: it was Lenin who built this architecture, and Stalin merely later took it and used it for his own political career. The Cheka was the secret police, which later became the more familiar KGB — surveillance, arrest, torture, execution. The host sums it up: when we look back at history we often say Stalin was a corrosive influence, that he brought the terror, but the architecture was in fact Lenin's bequest.

10:27 Tsaritsyn: Stalin arrested a front-line general
Trotsky appointed Snezarev, a general from the former tsarist army, to command the Tsaritsyn campaign — a textbook Trotsky move of using old officers, and one that put him directly in conflict with Stalin. Stalin, as political commissar, arrested the general and all his subordinate officers and locked them on a barge on the Volga. His intention, it is said, was to sink the boat and drown them. When Trotsky found out he was furious and ordered the general released immediately. This was the first round in the struggle between Trotsky and Stalin, and Trotsky won it decisively. But Stalin later told the story as one of the great civil-war battles in which he personally took the field, and Tsaritsyn was later renamed Stalingrad.

16:44 Whenever Stalin was unhappy he threatened to resign
Giles gives a detail that sits oddly with Stalin's later image: whenever things went badly — for instance when he wasn't authorised at Tsaritsyn to settle scores with Trotsky — he threatened to resign. He wrote a letter saying that without this, my work on the Southern Front would become meaningless and unnecessary, and that this gave him the right or the obligation to go even to the devil rather than remain on the Southern Front. The Politburo read the letter, grew tired of reading it, and then said, no, Joseph, stay, we all love you. He was a sulker. The picture fixes something in the reader's mind: the early Stalin used emotional blackmail, not terror.

29:12 Nobody at the time thought the General Secretary's job worth having
In April 1922 Stalin was appointed General Secretary. Today the title means supreme power in the state, but at the time it was just a functional description, tedious work. Stalin understood: handled properly, the post gave him complete control of the party. He could plant his own people in key positions and clear out everyone who supported Trotsky. From the day he took it over he made full use of the post, and already had one eye on the future — Lenin's health was poor, he was thinking about who would succeed Lenin, and now he had the chance to fill the party with supporters so that when Lenin died he would be in an advantageous position.

32:13 Stalin's apology: says sorry without admitting fault
Stalin telephoned Lenin's household. Lenin was gravely ill, and Stalin accused Nadezhda of discussing politics with Lenin as he was dying, saying it was unforgivable. Nadezhda told Lenin, Lenin was furious, and insisted Stalin write a letter of apology. The letter is superb: Stalin apologises without apologising — if you think I offended her, then I apologise, but I don't think I really offended her, so there is nothing to apologise for. Lenin grew even angrier. On 4 January 1923 Lenin wrote down his assessment of Stalin: Stalin is too rude, and this defect, entirely tolerable in our internal and comradely relations, becomes intolerable in the post of General Secretary; he therefore proposed that the comrades find a way to remove Stalin and replace him with someone else.

35:21 If Lenin hadn't died, Stalin would have put him in prison
Lenin's political life ended with his stroke, and he died ten days later. His wife, Nadezhda Krupskaya, said the most famous thing of all: if Lenin had not died in 1924, he would have been serving time in one of Stalin's prisons. She saw that Stalin was moving against Lenin as he rose. Giles thinks it very likely, because Stalin was absolutely ruthless towards anyone he believed was not on his side. Lenin wanted a simple burial; Stalin decided not to bury him but to embalm and preserve him and put him on permanent display. Within hours of Lenin's death they began draining the fluids and removing the organs, and the heart was never found again.

item.title: Solo Founders Aren't Alone: The Relationship Is the Product
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-solofounders-单人创始人不是一个人-关系才是产品/
item.description: 85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating finding relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.
item.content:encoded:
85% of startups die because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad. Being a solo founder really means being a solo artist — treating finding relationships as the main job, not actually carrying it all alone.

This episode has medium information density, but Dave Morin uses three cases — OpenClaw, Pulsia, and Ramble — to explain clearly what solo founders actually survive on. The mechanics in the back half are worth more than the motivational talk in the front half.

4:04 The share of solo-founded startups doubled in five years
Carta data shows that about 40% of companies this year were founded by a single person, up from less than 25% five years ago. Dave Morin doesn't think this is an accident: social media makes people feel not alone during nearly every waking hour, and AI has become a huge input source over the past two or three years. You used to lie in bed texting friends; now you talk to AI, explore your own ideas, and get input on what to do tomorrow. The "internal craft" of starting a company has also gone from a dark art held by a few people to something YouTube and ChatGPT can teach.

10:06 Most startups die from relationships, not products
Dave puts it directly: most startups fail because the relationship didn't work, not because the product idea was bad or the market didn't exist. He compares it to a band breaking up — you never get to hear the music you loved again. When your favorite app suddenly gets redesigned and the UI becomes infuriating, behind it is often that the "band" changed, the relationships changed, the people who made the thing changed. So he says the relationship is, in a sense, the product itself.

16:11 The design of the team matters as much as the design of the product
When Steve Jobs died, Dave was working on Path, Jony Ive was helping him, and he was also helping Jony with some Apple work. Jony told him something he still remembers: the design of the team matters as much as the design of the product. From that Dave derives his core judgment — you can be a solo artist, but you are always inside a huge collaboration, not just with the creators around you, but also with customers, listeners, and the community that cares about your product. You are not alone.

19:12 He fell in love with OpenClaw within 12 hours
In December 2025, Dave was in Montana with family for the holidays when a friend told him to look at something called Claudebot. He didn't look the first day; he installed it the second day, and in less than 12 hours he had that childhood feeling — when he was 7, his grandfather put a Macintosh on his desk, and for the first time he felt he could create anything. The second time he felt that was seeing Facebook; within 24 hours he decided he had to find the founder. This time it was OpenClaw, and he immediately went to find Peter, moving from Twitter DMs to iMessage, talking every day, saying, "I don't know what this will become, but everyone needs to experience it, and we have to protect it at all costs."

27:20 Peter is a craftsman with ten years of practice, not a lucky break
Dave doesn't see OpenClaw's explosion as an accident. Peter did ten years of hardcore PDF engineering and understands Mac OS details at the engineering level better than most people. So when Claude and agentic engineering appeared in 2025, he was an artist who had already fully digested all the material and could make his art extremely fast and extremely beautifully. Dave's conclusion: this is an extremely well-trained creator who, given new tools, made something magical.

32:24 Ben built himself a Company OS while traveling
After Ben and his co-founder decided not to be partners and split the company in two, he went alone to Kyoto, Hong Kong, Shanghai, and Thailand. Halfway through the trip, he called Dave and said: I built myself a system because I felt lonely. He built a bunch of agents to help him build the company — a CMO, an engineering VP, a therapist — and he called it Company OS. Dave says this was one of the earliest times he heard someone talk about multi-agent systems, more than a year ago. Three months later Pulsia launched. Ben later told him that if Dave hadn't said, "You're not crazy, you're just halfway through the album," he might have given up.

36:29 Matt applied data science to campsites
Matt's previous company was in book publishing, using data science and machine learning to reverse-engineer "what book you should write," selling books out before they even reached Amazon; at its peak, more than 80% of Amazon's top 50 books were published by them. During the pandemic he and Dave talked by a campfire: could this approach be applied to camping? National parks and Bureau of Land Management land can be camped on, but Airbnb has almost no supply in places like Zion. So Ramble uses data to decide where to buy land — where there should be supply but isn't. Dave calls this "the PhD mode of startups," because it's essentially real estate development, buying land, and negotiating with landowners, counties, and zoning boards.

44:32 You have to be the person in the world who loves it most
Dave says Matt is an extraordinary climber, at the level of climbing Denali, and he knows fewer than five people who do that kind of climbing. Ramble is an expression of Matt's love of nature; he wants to give other people that experience of being completely immersed in nature. Dave's inference: you have to love it that much to turn it into a business. Otherwise, first, someone else will love it more than you and they will beat you; second, you'll have to talk about it for ten thousand hours, and ten years later you'll still be talking about it, so you have to love it, because you'll have to eat ten thousand dinners about it.

item.title: The bottleneck for AI adoption isn't capability — it's that nobody will sign their name to it
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-latentspace-ai-落地的瓶颈不是能力-是没人敢签字担责/
item.description: Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.
item.content:encoded:
Waymo drove better than a human four years ago and still can't get into an airport — what constrains AI's usefulness was never capability, but liability, risk and trust. AIUC wants to fill that gap with standards plus insurance.

For founders and investors who care about AI adoption, compliance, insurance and third-party audit. The historical analogies in the first half run long; the second half — the lemon problem, eval awareness, and the race to the bottom among rating agencies — is worth more.

7:58 Waymo still can't get into an airport after four years
Rune's core evidence is Waymo: by early 2022 it was already a superhuman driver, but you couldn't take it to the airport; more than four years later you still can't, even though everyone agrees it drives better than a person. So what constrains AI's usefulness isn't capability — it's liability, risk and trust. Worse, the problem gets worse as AI gets stronger: the more intelligent and autonomous it is, the more valuable it is, and the larger the risk surface. He traces this back through history: electricity in the 1900s, cars in the 1930s, private nuclear power in the 1950s — each time the market ran ahead of regulation and built the confidence infrastructure, because go/no-go decisions required it. The shared blueprint is standards plus insurance: standards supply the rules of the road and which tests to run, insurers pay the claims, and therefore have the strongest incentive to genuinely quantify risk and find ways to reduce it.

23:26 Most companies have the right building blocks, but they don't work
Rune says the most important thing is that many companies have never done serious stress testing — they spend their time optimizing output quality in the good case and the average case, and they often hire their first security lead very late. Most companies actually have the right architecture and do have guardrails, either out of the box from the model vendor or filters they built themselves; the problem is that they don't work well. For example, dropping in a classifier that says "if this looks like medical advice, filter it out" — lots of companies have that, but the genuinely hard part is sitting down and thinking through all the ways someone could ask for medical advice, and reading the academic literature on the frameworks and tricks used to get around AI. AIUC-1 splits requirements into three categories: technical controls (for example, you must implement a groundedness filter), testing controls (tests must be run by an independent third party), and policy controls (for example, there must be a named person who owns the liability, and a plan for how customers get notified when something goes wrong).

38:14 Standards made by nonprofits are a problem
Rune says flatly that most standards in cybersecurity today are written by nonprofit organizations, and he thinks that's a problem. Nonprofits have no profit motive to hollow out a standard and race to the bottom on price, but by default they are completely unresponsive to the community they serve — there are no customers, nobody asking "what do you want," which is why satisfaction with existing security standards is generally low. He offers for-profit standards as counterexamples: Moody's, FICO credit scores, and earlier, crash-test standards that came from insurers; UL (Underwriters Laboratories) was born in an era when electric lights spread, houses caught fire, and insurers had to pay, and today UL has a for-profit entity, because serving customers well requires one. His conviction is that standards have to come before insurance: whether it's JPMorgan's CISO, Cursor's CISO or an underwriter at Lloyd's, the first demand is "don't have an incident" — once you've confirmed the risk is managed, insurance starts to mean something.

42:47 A policy is a trust signal to the market
Rune explains that demand for AI insurance comes mainly from the gap between "the people building AI" and "the people buying AI." Buying insurance isn't just about getting paid when something goes wrong; more importantly, the insurer brings trust: its willingness to underwrite says "there is risk here, but it's manageable," and its interests are aligned with the company adopting the AI, so it's a good signal to the market. When Waymo got its San Francisco operating permit, it went to multiple insurers and stacked them into a huge policy — not because Google couldn't afford the payout, but so that the government and a trusted third party would look at the data and say "we're willing to put some of this on our own balance sheet." The concrete case is ElevenLabs buying the first AI agent insurance policy, with Lloyd's of London as the third party looking at the data alongside them. There have been no claims yet.

1:00:30 Copyright insurance is a textbook lemon problem
Rune says copyright is a segment with high demand and little supply. One reason is that almost anyone who trained on copyrighted material knows they trained on it, so wanting to buy copyright infringement insurance is itself a signal that you're probably a high-risk customer — the people who most want to buy are exactly the ones most likely to have a copyright problem, which Swyx calls outright a lemon problem. Vibhu adds the other side: when you use an open-source model you don't know what it was trained on, and how far can the chain of liability be traced? Rune admits it's a hard problem and that he doesn't have the answer, but argues that "not unpacking open-source model training data line by line" is now treated as generally acceptable, so he won't hold you to a specific standard on it.

1:06:04 Agents are starting to know they're being evaluated
Rune points out that evals are facing a new challenge: agents are starting to realize they're being evaluated — eval awareness. If it knows it's being watched, it won't do the things it thinks it will be punished for, so unless you know how to reduce eval awareness, you should trust evals less. He thinks monitoring is the paradigm closer to the truth — did you actually give medical advice, how fast did you catch it, how often historically, how fast did you respond — at the cost of being more invasive, since it means looking at some customer data, but it will become more and more common. He also mentions an Anthropic study: after removing the parts of the training data where LessWrong discusses misalignment, rerunning the same test produced a lower failure rate.

1:12:56 The questions prediction markets can't answer are the audit business
Someone asks why not just open prediction markets on everything. Rune's answer: prediction markets depend on public information, but the information that actually drives high-stakes decisions is often private, or doesn't exist yet at all — for example, what a bank's security lead really needs to ask is "will this agent do the specific bad thing I care about in the specific scenario I care about," and that question has no answer anywhere. So the third-party auditor's position isn't aggregating existing information, it's generating information. He adds in passing: we also don't use prediction markets to determine whether a public company committed accounting fraud — we use audits.

1:14:02 Audit is a natural monopoly, but insurers can check it
Swyx cites the line from The Big Short where Moody's says "if I don't give you the AAA, you'll go to S&P" to make the point that rating agencies compete downward, and watchdogs naturally race to lower standards. Rune agrees, and gives the reason AIUC brought insurers into the picture — insurers are the one party without that dynamic, because they pay the claims directly, and driving the price down just means losing their own money. He also concedes there's no perfect system: Moody's needs scrutiny, and watchdogs need scrutiny too. Asked whether the business changes if, a year and a half from now, OpenAI's secret five-person group announces AGI, Rune says no, because the one thing a lab can never do is be its own watchdog — the problem isn't whether they care, it's that they're trapped in a race, with incentives to cut corners and withhold information from governments.

item.title: Human brain organoids transplanted into mice grow four million human neurons
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-naturepod-人脑类器官移植进小鼠-长出了四百万人类神经元/
item.description: Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons; their behaviour resembles neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice, but a third state.
item.content:encoded:
Mice genetically stripped of nearly their entire cortex, then given human brain organoids, grew about 4 million human neurons; their behaviour resembles neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice, but a third state.

The first half is solid neurodevelopmental research; the second half's "paper becomes an AI agent" workflow is more informative for people building research tools and AI agents.

2:08 No surgery — genetics makes the room
In 2022, Sergio Pasca's team implanted human brain organoids into newborn rat brains, but human brain cells grow far more slowly than rodent ones, and the implanted organoids were "outcompeted," unable to get connections or room to grow. This time they took a different approach: instead of surgery, they used genetics to delete a gene essential for cell division, only in the cells that would go on to form the brain region. The result was that cells preparing to build cortex the moment they were born could not divide and got stuck in place. The structure removed is called the pallium; it exists early on and later develops into the cerebral cortex and hippocampus. These "no-pallium mice" lost nearly half their brain volume but survived, with reduced body weight and largely normal basic motor and sensory responses.

4:08 Four million human neurons take over the empty space
The team injected human stem-cell-derived cortical organoids into no-pallium pups aged 5 to 17 days, about four organoids per injection, each roughly 100,000 cells, already differentiated and on their way to forming cortex. The human cells then divided, differentiated, were vascularised by the host, and mouse immune cells entered the interior of the human graft. Months later, the team estimated that these animals, called xenocortical mice, had about 70 million neurons in total, of which about 14 million were cortical and hippocampal cells, most of what had been removed now replaced by about 4 million human neurons. Human cells are larger and less dense, so the replacement is not an equal number, but it is still a very large number of human neurons.

6:10 They resemble neither normal mice nor cortex-less mice
The team used machine learning to analyse behavioural differences among three kinds of mice in video: controls, no-pallium mice that had lost almost the entire cortex, and xenocortical mice carrying the organoids. No-pallium mice differed clearly from controls, while xenocortical mice were "neither," sitting in a third behavioural state. Follow-up experiments backed this up: no-pallium animals had deficits on working-memory tasks, xenocortical animals did not. Sergio's judgement is that function was preserved in the animals that received human cortical cells, and the human cells very likely contributed some of it, but this is not perfect restoration — it only shows these cells can integrate functionally and produce behavioural consequences.

7:11 A hypoxia experiment shows it is the human cells doing the work
The team used this system to model brain injury. Hypoxia is severe in humans and can bring lifelong disease, whereas mice tolerate low oxygen far better. After the three kinds of mice were exposed to low-oxygen conditions for several hours, the human cells were induced to mount a hypoxia response, while the mouse brain was relatively resilient. Two days later, on a motor task, wild-type mice and no-pallium mice were fine, but the xenocortical mice carrying human cells began to show deficits in walking and gait coordination. Sergio thinks this shows it is very likely the human cells causing these deficits, and that this would be a powerful system, not only for asking about mechanism but for testing therapies — seeing whether there is benefit before going into clinical trials.

8:12 A very rare neuron type was grown
Aparna Bhaduri at the University of California studies human brain development and cancer, and she thinks one highlight of this work is that a cell type differentiated from the human organoids looks like a very rare kind of neuron that had previously been hard to culture in vitro. Loss of this neuron type is a key factor in a particular dementia, so understanding them better could help future therapy development. But she also points out there is a long way to go: the cortex's laminar structure and its different processing areas are not well preserved in this system, so it does not reach a more human-brain-like degree; and the authors themselves note that the developmental stage the organoids reach is still mid-development — this is not a fully mature cortex.

9:12 This is not a human brain in a mouse's head
Faced with the question of whether these animals count as human-mouse chimeras, Aparna Bhaduri says plainly: this is not a human brain inside a mouse. There are three reasons — it is immature; the complexity of cell types is insufficient, some cell types are still missing, and the cell types that are present are not mature; and although there are some connections with the rodent, the degree and the way they are routed differ from the human brain. So on complexity, maturity and connectivity, she considers this an organoid pushed forward in its development, not a human brain. Other researchers interviewed by Nature share this view: these are not fully formed functional human cortex.

10:13 Ethicists are not a stumbling block for scientists
Emily Jackson at the London School of Economics studies the regulation of stem-cell-related research, including brain organoids. She says the most striking thing about this paper, and about the work of Sergio Pasca's lab, is the team's focus on the importance of ethics and regulation. She thinks people sometimes mistakenly treat regulation as an obstacle to scientists, and that this is a genuine error: in her experience, scientists at the frontier of biotechnology very much want ethicists involved, very much want to know where the red lines are, so that they can proceed confident that society approves. She also stresses that when you replace part of a rodent's brain with human brain cells, the key question is what harm this does to the animal — especially a new kind of harm you might not easily notice — and that this must be taken very seriously.

17:19 Turning a paper into an agent you can talk to
James's team at Stanford proposes turning static papers into "knowledge agents," which you can think of as a paper's virtual corresponding author. Their workflow is called paper to agent: a set of AI agents reads the paper through, works out how it was done, reproduces the original results, then stores the knowledge in a server, acting as a translation layer between the human paper and any AI, so that models like ChatGPT and Claude become virtual co-authors you can ask anything about the paper — even run analyses with your own data. James stresses this differs from simply throwing the paper into a chatbot: the latter only reads, interprets and summarises results, does not know how the results and figures were generated, and cannot use the data and code, because it has no hands-on experience; a paper agent has that hands-on experience.

item.title: The Mess in AI Evaluation Isn't a Technical Problem, It's a Transparency Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-nejmaigrandrou-ai-评估的混乱不是技术问题-是透明度问题/
item.description: In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.
item.content:encoded:
In that 2019 systematic review, fewer than 5% of medical imaging AI papers met the rigor standards long established in other areas of medicine — and even the best-performing models only matched radiologists.

This episode has medium information density, but the first half — a first-hand account of how evidence standards in medical AI went from chaos to discipline — is directly useful to anyone building medical AI products.

11:22 Fewer than 5% of AI papers in top journals hold up
Around 2019, new papers appeared every week claiming "AI is as good as radiologists" or "AI beats radiologists at pneumonia detection," yet these conclusions contradicted each other. Xiao Liu and her collaborators did something no one was doing at the time: they applied the rigorous standards that the diagnostic test evaluation field had used for years to these AI papers, keeping only those with external validation, like-for-like comparisons, and meaningful control groups. The paper count was cut down sharply — fewer than 5% truly met the standards long established in other areas of medicine. And within that small handful, the best models only matched radiologists. This isn't bad news; it means there is too much noise in the published literature.

16:28 Reporting guidelines don't teach you how to do research, they force you to say what you did
CONSORT, SPIRIT, PRISMA, STARD and TRIPOD are essentially checklists specifying which items a paper must report. They don't tell you how to do the research — they are not methodology guidelines, they are transparency guidelines. Whether your methods are good or bad, you have to write them transparently and clearly. Their function is to put authors, journal editors and peer reviewers on the same information plane, with no smoke screens and nowhere to hide behind vague details. Xiao Liu adds a side effect: when authors know they must report a given item, it in turn forces methodological rigor upward, though that is hard to measure.

18:33 Guidelines come out of Delphi voting; items without consensus get cut
CONSORT AI and SPIRIT AI were not written by a few people behind closed doors; they went through a Delphi process: first a set of candidate items proposed through literature review and expert opinion, then multiple rounds of multi-stakeholder voting, closing with an in-person discussion. That in-person discussion is often the most valuable part, because people learn from each other. Items that fail to reach consensus are excluded; only those that reach consensus are kept. Xiao Liu says doing this kind of consensus project properly takes at least six months; she tried a rushed version compressed to three months, but participants contribute their time for free, and getting high-quality feedback and multi-round participation means you can't cut corners on time or reach.

20:36 Whether explainability belongs in reporting guidelines split the room
Andy Beam recalls that one question in the Delphi discussion was whether clinical trials should include explainability requirements, or at least report any explainability evaluation you did. He and Lauren Oakden-Rayner got up on the small stage and said "No, it shouldn't be done at all, and here's why." That debate was later commissioned as a paper by Lancet Digital Health editor Rupa, and became one of Andy's most cited papers. In the lightning round, Xiao Liu also clearly takes the "no" side: she argues you should first ask why you want AI to be explainable, and keep asking all the way down — what you ultimately want is just beneficial effects.

26:43 Advising regulators without ever working in industry felt insincere
At the time, Xiao Liu was doing academic AI research and clinical ophthalmology while increasingly consulting for regulators. She began to feel she had never stood on the side being regulated, and that consulting was a bit insincere. So she joined Apple as a health scientist, mainly designing validation studies for wearable device algorithms, such as Apple Watch sensing algorithms, including the hypertension notification feature released this year. She says Apple has a well-oiled product shipping machine, which was exactly the experience she wanted. After more than a year she returned to Birmingham to build a lab full time, and then joined Microsoft AI's newly formed medical frontier LLM team.

32:49 Short term computer scientists set the direction, long term clinicians gatekeep
Asked whether medical AI will be driven more by computer scientists or clinicians, Xiao Liu first pushed back on what "driven" means, and after confirming it meant "changed," gave her judgment: short term, computer scientists and engineers; long term, clinicians. The mechanism is that the people handling data, choosing metrics and choosing benchmarks determine in the short term which direction progress goes; but if the endpoint is real use on patients, clinicians will play the gatekeeper role at a later stage.

33:50 Doctors' work won't change much in five years, but should in ten
Xiao Liu thinks doctors' work won't look dramatically different within five years, but very likely will in ten years and beyond — and she hopes it will. The path she envisions: if medical intelligence and models keep advancing at the current pace, the medical profession no longer has to be about accumulating knowledge, or even about the kind of medical reasoning taught in medical school; the center of gravity shifts to being "a companion to experience" — accompanying deteriorating health, sudden health events, day-to-day wellbeing fluctuations, life-changing diagnoses, treatment failures and complications, and perhaps recovery, perhaps not. She believes people will continually need something deeply interpersonal on that journey: someone who can call on knowledge but doesn't necessarily carry it themselves, instead translating it into human language.

40:00 The most optimistic thing is dismantling old medical concepts; the most pessimistic is that we won't dare
Xiao Liu says she is more optimistic than pessimistic. What excites her most is that aggregating all the knowledge in the medical world may reveal that our understanding of biomarkers, disease phenotype clustering and existing medical knowledge frameworks is off. She gives her own doctoral research on inflammatory eye diseases as an example: a pile of diseases loosely called "white dot syndromes" just because they produce white dots in the fundus, but they are very likely driven by completely different mechanisms. She hopes one way new intelligence shows up is by dismantling these old concepts in medicine. The pessimistic side: the field is inherently cautious and may resist such dismantling out of unfamiliarity, sticking rigidly during a period of new technological change to the evaluation methods and guidelines of the past ten or twenty years, and missing the chance to discover.

item.title: He Treated Cancer With Bacterial Toxins and Was Dismissed by His Peers for Forty Years
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-stuffmissed-他用细菌毒素治癌症-被同行骂了四十年/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he could not standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and radiation and regulation pushed it out; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around it.
item.content:encoded:
Coley used streptococcal toxins to make tumors vanish in some sarcoma patients, but he could not standardize the treatment or explain its mechanism, and radiation and regulation pushed it out; his daughter spent the second half of her life building a cancer research institute around it.

Medium information density: the first half is medical-history background, but the second half — on why the therapy was abandoned and how immunotherapy picked up the thread — is where the value is.

6:13 The death of an 18-year-old patient changed him
In 1890, Coley took on 17-year-old Bessie Dashiell, who had persistent pain after injuring her hand and was eventually diagnosed with periosteal sarcoma. Coley amputated below the elbow, but the tumor soon appeared elsewhere, and she died on January 23, 1891, at just 18 years old, only about 10 weeks after Coley first examined her. Coley was 28, in his first year as a surgeon. Amputation was the only treatment he could offer, and it had not worked, which sent him digging through roughly 90 records of cancer surgery patients at New York Hospital from the previous 15 years, looking for something better.

7:15 In one record, the tumor disappeared on its own
In the case files, Coley found a case of small round cell sarcoma of the neck in a patient of his colleague Dr. William T. Bull: four recurrences, and by the fifth operation the tumor had invaded deep structures and could not be removed. After surgery the patient accidentally developed erysipelas of the face and neck, then had a second attack two weeks later. Within days of the first attack the tumor began to soften and shrank rapidly, and by discharge it had disappeared completely. The hospital had no follow-up record, so Coley went door to door in the German immigrant community and found him: in the spring of 1891 he was still alive, with no local or systemic recurrence, seven years after the operation.

9:21 He tried live bacteria first, then switched to toxins
On May 2, 1891, Coley began trying to induce erysipelas in a patient with inoperable sarcoma of the tonsil and neck. The tumor was so large the patient could not eat solid food and could swallow only small amounts of liquid. Coley exposed the patient to bacteria cultured in the lab, but for months could not induce erysipelas, until October, when he injected a culture a colleague had brought back from Robert Koch's laboratory in Germany. The patient became very ill, but two weeks later the neck tumor had disappeared and the tonsil tumor had shrunk, and the patient lived in good health for eight years. By the end of 1892, after two early patients died of infection, Coley began working with bacteriologists to heat-kill the bacteria and filter out the toxins rather than use live bacteria directly.

15:34 The effect was real, but only in some patients
In his papers, Coley wrote that in his own experience, in slightly more than 10% of cases the regression process continued until the tumor was completely absorbed and the patient remained cured; in other cases the improvement was only temporary, and within weeks the tumor regrew and the patient died despite continued injections at higher doses; and in a very few cases, especially large, highly vascular tumors, particularly the melanotic type, no clearly beneficial effect was ever observed. By 1909 he was recommending it for all inoperable sarcomas (except the melanotic type), for osteosarcoma of the long bones where surgery meant sacrificing a limb, for primary sarcoma after the surgical wound had healed as a preventive against recurrence, and for all carcinomas after surgery, using the mixed toxins to reduce recurrence.

19:40 JAMA waited, then declared failure two months later
On May 31, 1894, Coley read his paper before the American Surgical Association. In October of that year, JAMA published a piece comparing bacterial toxins to diphtheria antitoxin, saying the best method of use had not yet been determined, that it was still experimental, and calling for patience until experts produced complete results. But only two months later, on December 15, 1894, JAMA published "The Failure of the Erysipelas Toxins," saying there was "no longer much question that toxin injections as a cure for sarcoma and malignant growths have completely failed," that many surgeons had faithfully tried it over the previous six months, and that not one fully verified recovery had been reported. Coley responded the following January, noting that he had used not only erysipelas toxins but also Bacillus prodigiosus, and that the failure of a few doctors in a limited number of cases would not settle the scientific community's judgment of whether the method succeeded.

23:47 Forty years, a thousand patients, a hundred and fifty papers
Coley worked with these toxins for about 40 years, treated roughly 1,000 cancer patients, and published about 150 papers. In 1909 he wrote that 52 cases of inoperable sarcoma had been successfully treated with a mixed toxin of erysipelas and Bacillus prodigiosus, of which 35 remained healthy for 3.25 to 16 years, 28 for 5 to 16 years, and 14 for 10 to 16 years. Although Park, Davis, and Company had been producing various preparations since 1899, the toxins never became the most common treatment for inoperable sarcoma. The reasons included: tense relations with his boss James Ewing, who opposed his research; the bone sarcoma registry refusing to include his cured patients, insisting they had been misdiagnosed; his insistence that all cancers had a microbial origin, even after that idea had been overturned; the difficulty of producing and standardizing the toxins; and the 1902 Biologics Control Act, which raised the regulatory cost.

26:54 Radiation took his window of time
Coley's own method of use was also fairly loose: different patients received different doses by different methods for different lengths of time. Partly this was because he was trying to work out what worked and how best to do it, but some treatment decisions were made almost on feel rather than data. He also noted that other doctors using his toxins treated patients for much longer than he did, conceding that his own shorter courses might explain some patients' recurrences. X-rays were discovered in 1895 and radium in 1898, and radiation quickly became the standard treatment for many inoperable cancers. Both discoveries came early in his writing about the therapy. In 1934, JAMA published a statement from its Council on Pharmacy and Chemistry that was slightly more positive in wording than 40 years earlier, saying the mixed toxins of erysipelas and prodigiosus might sometimes play an important role in preventing or delaying malignant recurrence or metastasis, and might occasionally cure hopeless inoperable tumors. But by then Coley had already retired, and he died on April 16, 1936, at the age of 74.

29:00 His daughter spent her life building an institute for him
After Coley died, his daughter Helen Coley Nauts began organizing his papers and correspondence, intending to write a biography, and ended up digging deep into his work. She had no medical qualifications and no formal education beyond high school, but she carefully went through all of her father's publications, trying to work out what separated the successes from the failures. In 1953, with the philanthropist Oliver R. Gray Sr., she founded the Cancer Research Institute, with funding from sources including Nelson Rockefeller. She served as its director until her death in 2001. Her brother Bradley was also an advocate of their father's method and became chief of bone surgery at Memorial Hospital after their father retired. The Cancer Research Institute today has an award named after Coley, recognizing outstanding research in basic and tumor immunology.

item.title: Government Doesn't Just Waste Your Money — It Wastes an Hour of Your Week
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-tyler-政府不只浪费你的钱-还浪费你每周一小时/
item.description: Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.
item.content:encoded:
Plenty of countries file taxes for their citizens; the IRS is legally barred from doing it for you. The time tax hits the poor, immigrants and the formerly incarcerated hardest — and AI may not save them.

Medium information density, but the "time tax" frame itself is valuable: it reprices the administrative friction of the welfare state as a regressive levy. The confession in the back half about a shifting stance on UBI is worth hearing.

0:58 The IRS is legally barred from filing your taxes for you
Lowrey's central example: in Japan, salaried workers never touch the tax process at all; many countries mail you a pre-filled return and you just correct the errors. The US could easily do this — nine in ten households take the standard deduction, and their tax situations are fairly simple — but the IRS is not legally permitted to. This is not a technology problem, it's an institutional choice. She defines the "time tax" as the portion of cost the government shifts onto individuals as administrative labour, and unlike a monetary tax it works differently: you can earn more money, you cannot earn more time.

1:02 The worst program is TANF, not the IRS
Lowrey names TANF (cash welfare) the single worst program in government: it nominally exists to address child poverty, in practice it does not move the child poverty rate, its compliance burden is extremely heavy and punitive, and its $16.5 billion a year is essentially wasted. She offers a rule — programs aimed at high-income Americans are a far better experience, safety-net programs are broadly bad, and welfare is the worst. This yields a counterintuitive judgment: the quality of government service is inversely proportional to the political influence of its beneficiaries.

6:08 Pandemic fraud is not something the time tax can prevent
Cowen raises a common objection: after deregulation in 2020 fraud exploded, so maybe the time tax is the necessary cost of fraud prevention. Lowrey rejects this outright: the fraud came mainly from criminal rings and fake small businesses, and from the fact that UI systems themselves run on ancient COBOL infrastructure. Her mechanism is misaligned incentives — governors have no incentive to upgrade UI systems when unemployment is low, so the same conversation repeats every recession. The conclusion: building state capacity and agile digital systems prevents fraud; pushing the work onto individuals does not.

11:19 Large-scale fraud is almost entirely on the supply side
Lowrey points out that fraud in Medicare and Medicaid is almost entirely on the provider side: nursing homes, clinics and hospital systems defrauding the government. The ceiling on individual fraud is low, because the money you can extract from the government is limited; to commit large-scale fraud you have to process a lot of transactions. So her policy ordering is: reduce administrative overhead in other programs, concentrate enforcement resources on criminal organisations and legitimate providers, rather than loading burdens onto the 99.9% who don't commit fraud. She adds a piece of political economy: fraud narratives are often used to make programs look illegitimate, so voters tolerate cuts.

13:25 Fifty hours per person per year, and highly unequal
Lowrey's quantitative estimate comes from the American Time Use Survey: total bureaucratic time is about 50 hours per person per year, close to an hour a week. She concedes the number is understated — ATUS cannot capture multitasking (cooking while on hold is recorded as one activity), and time taxes are scattered across categories and never totalled. Who pays the most? People entangled with the criminal justice system, immigrants, the poor. The rich can "skip" it with staff and accountants — with one exception: a permit to renovate a house in San Francisco means waiting 500 days and going through multiple rounds of public review no matter how rich you are.

22:57 AI can fill out forms, but it can't fill a urine test
Cowen asks whether AI agents could handle all of this within five years. Lowrey says probably, but raises two caveats: first, the users of the most burdensome programs are low-income, and whether they know about or trust these agents is unknown; second, much of the burden isn't paperwork at all — it's mandatory interviews, urine screening, data that is hard to collect. She gives SNAP as an example: benefits are calculated by household, and the government has no stable definition of "household", so you have to explain how you and your co-residents split the cost of staple food — the kind of question AI struggles to answer for you too. She notes she was originally sceptical, but a civic technologist who has worked in this field for years firmly believes AI will help a great deal.

31:18 Disability insurance is already hard enough to apply for
Cowen presses with data: the number of people on disability insurance rose about fourfold between 1990 and 2014, while workplace deaths kept falling — shouldn't the threshold be raised? Lowrey doesn't accept the inference. She offers two alternative explanations: population ageing and the rise of obesity-related chronic illness. Then the counter-evidence: 5% of applicants have to submit more than 1,000 pages of medical material; 11,000 Americans die each year while waiting for a disability determination. She admits she worries about both directions — about paying people who don't need it, and about rejecting people who genuinely do — so she doesn't think this is the moment to add more paperwork.

38:28 The research moved her position on UBI
Lowrey's previous book, Give People Money, was pro-UBI; here she says plainly that the research findings are "sobering", and that she has updated her priors: the side benefits she expected cash to deliver did not materialise. Her defence, though, is that the point of giving people money is to give people money to buy things, and that rationale still holds; life improving less than expected is not an argument against the policy. On AI and UBI, she admits she was extremely dismissive back then of the claim that "AI will force UBI", and she won't go that far now — but if GDP and productivity surge while unemployment rises at the same time, that would be very strange, and it would be time to start considering UBI-type policies.

item.title: After Tome Hit 25 Million Users, He Tore It Down to Build a CRM
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-a16z-tome-做到-2500-万用户后-他推倒重来去做-crm/
item.description: Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he bets the CRM is won not by making salespeople do more work, but by whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.
item.content:encoded:
Keith Perez walked away from Tome and its 25 million users because his own team didn't like the product; he bets the CRM is won not by making salespeople do more work, but by whether you can fully model a company's customer reality.

The first half is a rare post-mortem on deliberately shutting down a growing product; the second half is dense, hands-on detail on pricing, expansion and org design.

3:01 They killed a hit not on data, but on dislike
Tome launched alongside ChatGPT and reached 2 million users a month, so many that inference capacity ran short and people had to queue. But Keith says what actually made them stop wasn't a metric — it was that "none of us liked the product." Concretely: they couldn't see a path where a picky, high-quality presentation maker would treat Tome as indispensable, nor one where investment banking or consulting people would write memos in it. Their conclusion was that what the models lacked wasn't general reasoning ability but context about who the presenter is, who the audience is, and what relationship holds between them — and that gap wouldn't close just by waiting for better models.

6:04 Follow the heat first, then find the real problem is data
The Tome team dug through its own user base and found B2B users clustered in sales and marketing, so they gave free pilots to 12 large companies. The original goal was helping sales build new-business decks and proposals, but customers started asking: can you also do research, help us qualify leads, help us understand which companies are worth expanding into. They followed that pull, asking customers to open up access to CRM, call recordings and data warehouses, and found the hardest part wasn't doing that work — it was that the data in those systems contradicted itself. The reality in call recordings and the reality in the CRM often didn't line up. Keith says reorganizing that data started to look like the most important work, so they concluded: if you can reorganize a company's reality into something both machines and people understand, that's more worth doing than the original path.

8:11 Nobody wants your four-month-old CRM, so pay them
What they built first was a go-to-market assistant that AEs used every day but that they couldn't charge for — the data wasn't theirs, and ten other companies were chasing the same thing. So they cut headcount, rethought the CRM from scratch, worked in stealth for four months, and then discovered nobody wanted a four-month-old CRM. The only asset left was a huge office lease they couldn't get out of, so they posted on X and LinkedIn: use our CRM and we'll let you sit in our office for free. That's "negative pricing." The 10 startups they brought in were there every day, complaining about slowness and missing features, but giving feedback in Slack every two hours. Keith says this was the exact opposite of Tome: a barely working product that users were inside every day and cared enough about to give hourly feedback.

11:21 The core of a CRM is relationships, not fields
Three of Lightfield's five founders came from Facebook. Their plain judgment was that the most important thing in a CRM is modeling relationships, so they borrowed directly from the Facebook timeline and built an activity log first — when you first made contact, what you said, what they replied, which meetings happened, which documents went back and forth — eventually extending to what the other party did inside your product and how they paid. Every traditional CRM field update and stage advance is triggered off that log, but underneath there is always a canonical relationship log. They also tried going fully unstructured and found queries too slow, a needle-in-a-haystack problem, and landed on semi-structured: stuff large amounts of unstructured data into the activity log and let the system infer causality from it.

15:26 Get the data model wrong and sales won't go back and fix it
They interviewed a lot of CRM consultants, asking what they actually do for clients, and found the highest-consequence thing is the data model: set your stages and fields wrong and you can't send salespeople back in time to fill in the data — it's over. So Lightfield chose to be schema-less: connect email, drop in a call recording, hook up the data warehouse, and the system assembles the relationship in real time; fields come later. Change your mind and it walks the activity log and backfills. Alex Rampell compressed this into "intelligence is greater than schema," and contrasted it with the old era: back then, to save space, every column in a table had to have a predefined varchar length, like name varchar 25 — now they don't even want a schema.

17:28 Someone used it to find frontier treatment for an Alzheimer's patient
Because it supported fully arbitrary schemas, custom objects and custom relationships from the start, Lightfield attracted a set of customers with very strange business models. Keith's example is Power: on one side it serves pharma companies, helping them find clinical trial subjects; on the other it's a marketplace aggregating patients with hard-to-diagnose conditions and hunting for frontier treatments. They modeled both the B2C and B2B sides in Lightfield, wrote automations to scrape the FDA and clinicaltrials.gov, built a world model of every ongoing clinical trial on earth, and then matched patients to pharma companies. The result: Lightfield actually helped an Alzheimer's patient find frontier treatment within days.

23:37 Win the founders and engineers first, wait for the sales VP to come around
Alex points out something often overlooked: the sales VP a greenfield company hires was trained by Salesforce and will say flat out, "I don't use that." Lightfield's design principle is to win first the founders, engineering leads and product leads — the people willing to use frontier technology to understand customers — while making every sales-led capability free for anyone in the company to use. That both helps the company understand what engineering, support and finance are doing and creates real intra-company network effects that make replacement harder. When that senior sales VP arrives and finds engineering, finance and support all using it for customer understanding and account scoring, the company pushes him to try it, and that's when they get their opening.

32:00 Pure seat-based and pure consumption pricing both blew up
They tried pure seat-based pricing first; acceptance was decent, but top users consumed 10,000 times what the tail did, which doesn't work long term. Then they tried pure consumption pricing, turning everything into credits, and within three weeks nobody touched any feature — Keith calls it the company's worst three weeks, lots of signups and no usage. Finally they split it into four kinds of work: everyday CRM work (logging meetings, filling fields, updating tasks) goes into a platform fee or seat fee, because customers don't want to budget annually for "the margin of error on core CRM"; pipeline generation is charged on consumption, because there's alpha there that turns into revenue; workflow automation is charged separately, e.g. someone requests a demo on your site and Lightfield decides this is a deep tech company that should go to Henry and that one is health tech that should go to Matt; and finally intelligence and prediction, which Keith considers Lightfield's most untapped part, where customers will pay for the alpha.

item.title: Are bad teeth the number one reason kids go to A&E? The number got misread
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-moreorless-儿童看急诊第一原因是牙-数字被念错了/
item.description: A British MP said teeth are the top reason children end up in A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.
item.content:encoded:
A British MP said teeth are the top reason children end up in A&E. The actual figure refers to 5-to-18-year-olds hospitalised for tooth decay — not the same thing, and the decay rate is actually drifting down.

Four fact-checks strung into one episode: fast pace, medium information density. The teeth and medicines segments have the most solid numbers; the NEET and P-Doom segments work better as thinking exercises.

1:01 Teeth are the top reason for A&E visits — that claim is wrong
Leila Moran, a Liberal Democrat MP and chair of the Health and Social Care Committee, said on Radio 4's The World at One that teeth are the number one reason children go to A&E. Chris Venatza, a consultant in paediatric dentistry at Newcastle University, flatly rejected it: she very likely conflated two sets of numbers. What actually ranks first is "hospital admission for tooth decay treatment" — the number one reason 5-to-18-year-olds are admitted to hospital. A&E visits, by contrast, have all sorts of causes, and there is simply no data showing whether dentistry ranks high or low among them. Moran's office later confirmed Chris was right, and that she had meant the hospital admission figure, not the A&E figure.

3:09 Lots of hospital tooth extractions, because the rules changed in 2001
When children are hospitalised for their teeth, it is usually for an extraction, not a filling. Extractions are harder for a child to endure, so children who cannot cooperate for an extraction in a dental clinic may need a general anaesthetic. There is an institutional turning point here: the rules changed in 2001, and ordinary dental practices were no longer allowed to administer general anaesthesia, so anyone needing it had to go to hospital. So a large share of the hospital admission numbers are extractions under general anaesthetic. That explains why "hospital admission" and "A&E" are two entirely different measures — one is a surgical arrangement pushed into hospitals by the rules, the other is an unplanned visit.

4:10 The admission rate is actually falling, not a crisis
Chris gave the admission rate per 100,000 population: about 320 in 2015, down to 270 before the pandemic, and 250 now. Host Tim Harford's reaction was that "this doesn't look like a crisis, the trend is even quite encouraging." Chris acknowledged that falling before the pandemic was a good thing, but stressed that even so, large numbers of children are still having general anaesthetics and dental treatment in hospital, which is not good in itself. He added one more thing: for the past decade, dental causes have been the number one reason for hospital admission, unchanged for ten years — so the "number one" position is stable, but the absolute level is heading down.

5:10 To see the decay rate, look at school surveys, not admissions
Chris said that if you want to understand the real state of children's tooth decay, there are better datasets: the government sends dentists into schools to examine five-year-olds. The latest survey found 22% of five-year-olds already have decay reaching the dentine layer — close to a quarter. He said that a quarter of the population having a disease that needs treatment is not a good state of affairs. Over time: about 30.9% in 2008, down to 23% in 2017-2018, then a plateau, with the latest survey slightly down again from the 2022 one. Longer-term data comes from a survey run once a decade since 1973: 72% of five-year-olds had decay in 1973, down to 43% in 2003 — roughly halved.

8:15 25% of UK medicines come from Israel — off by two orders of magnitude
US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said on the Today programme that 25% of the medicines Britain uses are made in Israel. Lizzie McNeill checked the latest ONS import data: in 2025 the UK imported £10 million of medicines from Israel, against total UK medicine imports of about £28 billion, so Israel accounts for just 0.04% — one twenty-fifth of 1%, not 25%. She also ruled out several possibilities: active pharmaceutical ingredients come mainly from India and China, and the more upstream raw materials mainly from China; and medicines supplied by Israeli companies (the biggest being Teva) are mostly not made in Israel but in European plants in Hungary, Croatia and elsewhere. Teva estimates it supplies one in eight generic medicine packs in the UK, equivalent to one-ninth of all prescriptions, but the other Israeli companies are all too small to push the total to 25%.

13:29 Blame Gove for rising NEETs, and Wales dismantles the case
Education Secretary Lucy Powell wrote in The Times that a million young people have been left behind by the education system Michael Gove led. Daisy Christodoulou rebutted with a natural experiment: Wales and Scotland took the opposite path to Gove's reforms. Wales's NEET rate for 16-to-24-year-olds rose from 14% in 2019 to 17% in 2025, while England's rose from 11% to 13% over the same period — similar levels, similar trends, with Wales rising slightly more. If Gove is responsible for England's rise, then Wales must be responsible for Wales's rise, yet the two sides' policies are completely opposite. She said the NEET rate sits on top of economic structure, the minimum wage, taxes, regulation and far too many other factors — not just education.

17:51 Teen mental health is sliding, and not only in England
Responding to the criticism that Gove's reforms increased academic pressure and damaged mental health, Daisy looked at the WHO's Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey, which reports England, Scotland and Wales separately. The results show average life satisfaction among teenagers fell in all three nations this century (2000 to 2022), but it also fell across Western Europe and in many other regions, so it is not specific to England. Then the share of 15-year-olds who "like school a lot": about 10% in England, about 9% in Scotland, about 7.5% in Wales — all low, but essentially the same across the three. The share of 15-year-olds feeling overwhelmed by academic pressure is high in all three, with no big difference.

19:59 P-Doom is a subjective probability, and nobody can produce a model
Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, warning that Anthropic and OpenAI are irresponsible on AI safety. Anthropic's Evan Hubinger responded on X: he personally thinks the probability that AI kills all of humanity within the next decade is greater than 10%. Alexander Mark Koch, an assistant professor of global risk and resilience at Cambridge, explained that P-Doom is shorthand for "the probability that AI causes human extinction," and that it is almost always one individual's subjective probability estimate. He said the issue is extraordinarily complex: it involves regulatory capacity, system resilience, where large-model capabilities are heading, autonomous weapons and biotech tools, whether AI can self-improve into an exponential loop, funding, rules, what China will do, and disaster scenarios ranging from science fiction to "a rogue state using a large model to learn to make bioweapons."

item.title: Sequoia's Former Boss on Reading People: What Happens Before Age 14 Sets Your Core
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ilt-红杉前掌门看人-14-岁前发生了什么-内核就定了/
item.description: Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you unconsciously absorb from your parents before you are 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.
item.content:encoded:
Digging into his own refugee family's history, he found that the imprint you unconsciously absorb from your parents before you are 12, 13, 14 stays with you for life; what changes afterward is the external intensity, not the core.

Not an investing lesson but a retrospective on origins, reading people, and writing. The back half — on structural shifts in venture and the great man theory of history — is the most valuable; the family history up front is more personal.

7:23 The grandfather who waited for the situation to pass vanished
Moritz's two grandfathers were two responses to the same catastrophe. His maternal grandfather was a lower-court judge in Bavaria, had fought at Verdun in World War I, believed in the durability of the state, and had a pension he was unwilling to give up, so he delayed leaving, and in the end he and his wife were sent east and disappeared from history. The other grandfather was nearly blind, supported his family alone by trading cattle, had no pension to wait for, and left with his wife 72 hours before the war broke out — three days later and they too would have died. Moritz says the lesson he draws is not a moral judgment but that you must always have a bolt hole to hide in, and you can never have too many passports.

21:03 His most effective question makes people cry on the spot
When he interviews people he always asks one fixed question: looking back, if there were one thing, one action you could have done differently, what would it be. He remembers a person interviewing at Sequoia bursting into tears when asked this — the man was the son of Latino immigrants, and at around age 12 he and a friend stole candy from a corner grocery store; the owner told his father, who dragged him back to the store by the ear and made him apologize and empty his pockets. Years later, asked this question, the first thing he thought of was still the shame he had brought on his family. Moritz says many people conducting interviews are not really listening to the answers.

26:03 He sorted everyone he knew into categories on Zoom
Inspired by a series about a French village in World War II, he divided people into three categories: resisters, the silent, and collaborators. During the pandemic, in those Zoom meetings with a dozen little windows, he would stare at each person he knew and think: if these people had lived in a French village in the 1940s, who would stay silent, who would resist, who would collaborate. He says resisters are always a tiny minority, because bad things happen in a country precisely because most people stay silent. Asked how many of the people he has invested in would be resisters, he says he would like to think so, but he is not sure.

38:04 The painter gave himself one day off a year
Frank Auerbach was a refugee from Nazi Germany, and Moritz calls him a complete monomaniac: apart from one day off each Christmas to rest at Brighton Pier, he painted every single day. His models were a small fixed group of people, the same few faces painted for decades; one model who lived in Venice flew to London once a week to sit for him. His wife's house was right on the English coast, and Moritz asked whether he went there; he answered: I have never been to that house. From this Moritz discusses the cost of monomania — the cost to relationships is almost inevitable, but sometimes great things come out of exactly that.

43:04 He bet on something beyond the résumé
Around 1985, Moritz was still a journalist and wrote to five small funds looking for a job. Everyone except Don Valentine told him he had no technical background, no engineering degree, no experience at a tech company, and suggested he go into PR or marketing. Don was willing to take the risk, for a straightforward reason: he had seen several people with operating backgrounds at large tech companies move into investing and fail, and he had also seen several who succeeded — an actuary, and the one he cited most, Arthur Rock: an investment banker by background, with nothing in his résumé that predicted success. Don did not believe in teaching people; he believed in throwing them into the deep end and seeing whether they drowned.

46:15 Venture's old advantage was imperfect information
Moritz says doing venture in the 1980s and 90s had several advantages that have now disappeared, the first being imperfect information: before the internet, unless you were close to something you did not know what was happening, whereas now the whole world basically gets the same information. The second is that the early market has far too many participants — individuals, two- or three-person funds, giant mutual funds — too many intermediaries, and it is no longer possible for investors to build the kind of real, close relationship with founders they once had. He therefore says a moderately intelligent, quick-minded 14- to 16-year-old could have done venture in the mid-80s; he is not sure he could still do it well today.

52:57 He believes in the great man theory without apology
Asked whether it is great individuals or enduring institutions that shape the course of history, Moritz's answer is blunt: he is a firm believer in the great man theory. From Lee Iacocca to Steve Jobs, from politics to the battlefield, what matters is great leaders; and of course also tyrants who cast a shadow over tens of millions of people for decades. In his work at Sequoia and in writing Ferguson, he cares about the same thing — how an organization stays alive across decades. And on Elon, he says he is completely stunned by the scale of his achievements across several different industries, and thinks he may be the greatest industrialist in American history.

58:40 The more AI writes, the more valuable a human voice becomes
Moritz says that because AI can easily produce vast amounts of text, excellent writing that cuts through the garbage is actually appreciating in value; his definition of excellent writing is ‘a voice you can hear that cannot be mistaken for anyone else's’. The hardest thing for a writer is to get close enough to your own inner feeling and voice that it outweighs the weight of others' expectations — he quotes Joseph Campbell: the privilege of a lifetime is to become who you truly are, and that is also the hardest thing. He does not consider himself a technologist, and says AI is rarely discussed at home; on employment he is optimistic: people predicted doom when the atomic bomb exploded, and predicted a genetic revolution creating humans in the 1970s, and neither happened, and this time he thinks more jobs will be created than destroyed.

item.title: The strongest El Niño hasn't peaked yet, but no one alive has seen one this big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ologies-最强厄尔尼诺还没到峰值-但没人活着见过它这么大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-16-ologies-最强厄尔尼诺还没到峰值-但没人活着见过它这么大/
item.description: The 2026 El Niño already exceeded the peaks of the two strongest events on record, 1982 and 2015, by autumn — and its peak usually doesn't arrive until winter. This is not a climate forecast for the future; it is weather that is happening now.
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 El Niño already exceeded the peaks of the two strongest events on record, 1982 and 2015, by autumn — and its peak usually doesn't arrive until winter. This is not a climate forecast for the future; it is weather that is happening now.

Meteorologist Marshall Shepherd lays out the mechanics of El Niño, how it's observed, and what it actually does — and unpacks how a UN report got misread by the media as a "strategic retreat." High information density, worth listening to.

5:24 The UN didn't say retreat — a reporter said it first
On September 2, 2026, the UN Environment Programme published a report titled "Limiting Overshoot." AP reporter Seth Borenstein wrote "strategic retreat" in the first sentence of his story, and the phrase was copied into headlines worldwide, turning into an end-of-the-world narrative of "we're done for." But the word "retreat" does not appear in the report at all — the UN was in fact doubling down on emissions cuts. What was actually abandoned was only the claim that 1.5 degrees can still be held.
